:::: cols
::: {}
Every project in this course goes round this cycle, from HW1 to your group project.

- **Exploration and analysis** go round and round: look, test, look again.
- To answer more, go back: **fetch more data**, or **refine the question**, and round again.
- **Reproducible** is not a last step: it frames every step.
- Your report follows the cycle, and ends with *How to reproduce*.

# Are baby names a fashion? {.divider}

<p class="muted">Small project · one source</p>

## The workflow

::: workflow
<div><span class="kicker">Data</span><b>Statistics Sweden (SCB)</b>
<ul><li>downloaded straight from their database by a short script</li><li>how many people born each year 1922–2021 have each of the 200 most common names</li></ul></div>
<div><span class="kicker">Cleaning</span><b>A tidy table</b>
<ul><li>reshape the table so it is easy to work with</li><li>handle the gaps: SCB hides very small numbers</li><li>turn counts into shares, so years can be compared</li></ul></div>
<div><span class="kicker">Analysis</span><b>Find the comebacks</b>
<ul><li>plot each name over 100 years</li><li>a comeback score: common in the 1920s, rare in 1960–80, common again after 2005</li></ul></div>
<div class="result"><span class="kicker">Results</span><b>Yes, with a catch</b>
<ul><li>Ella, Elsa, Alice, Astrid, Ebba top the score</li><li>the top 10 names: 59% of a year in 1922, 24% in 2021</li><li>only the living are counted</li></ul></div>
:::

<p class="wfcode"><code>names/fetch.py</code> → <code>names/data/</code> → <code>names/report.qmd</code> → <code>report.md</code><span>one command: <code>uv run quarto render</code></span></p>

::: notes
The whole project in one slide: where the data came from, what we did to it, what we found.
The next slides show the result and the catch.
:::

## Names skip three generations

<img src="../../img/introduction/names-comebacks.svg" alt="Share of births named Elsa, Alice and Astrid, 1922–2021: high in the 1920s, almost zero in 1960–80, high again after 2000">

<p class="small">Share of each birth year with the name, among the 200 most common names in Sweden. Data: SCB.</p>

::: notes
Common in the 1920s, nearly gone around 1970 (grey band), back after 2000. Ask: who in the room
has a grandmother or great-grandmother called Elsa, Alice or Astrid?
:::

## The catch: only the living are counted

```{=html}
{{< include ../../public/img/introduction/diagram-survivors.svg >}}
```

- The table counts people **alive in Sweden in 2021**, by year of birth: the dead and the emigrated are gone.
- It only lists names common **today**, so a 1920s name that never came back is missing.
- The data is tilted towards finding comebacks. **Saying so is part of the result.**

::: notes
Survivorship bias. This is the step where the real thinking was in this project: the
conclusion and its limitation. A small project with an honest limitation is a good project.
:::

## The maths: a comeback score

For each name $n$ and birth year $t$, the **share** of people born that year with the name:

$$s_{n,t} = \frac{\text{people born in year } t \text{ called } n}{\text{people born in year } t \text{ with any of the 200 names}}$$

Average the share over three periods, $\bar s_{\text{1920s}}$ (1922–35), $\bar s_{\text{dip}}$ (1960–80) and $\bar s_{\text{now}}$ (2005–21). A comeback is big when **both** popular periods dwarf the dip:

$$\text{score}(n) = \min\left( \frac{\bar s_{\text{1920s}}}{\bar s_{\text{dip}}},\ \frac{\bar s_{\text{now}}}{\bar s_{\text{dip}}} \right)$$

<p class="small">Elsa: $\min\left(\frac{3.06\%}{0.034\%}, \frac{1.72\%}{0.034\%}\right) = \min(90, 51) = 51$.<br>A name absent in the dip counts as 0.01%, so we never divide by zero.</p>

::: notes
Why the minimum: a name that was only popular in the 1920s, or only now, should not count as a
comeback. The minimum is large only if both ratios are large.
:::

# Why does electricity cost more in Malmö than in Luleå? {.divider}

<p class="muted">Medium project · two sources combined</p>

## The workflow

::: workflow
<div><span class="kicker">Data</span><b>Two free online sources</b>
<ul><li>electricity prices for the four zones, every hour for three years</li><li>SMHI: wind and temperature in Malmö</li><li>downloaded by a script and saved, so anyone can rerun it</li></ul></div>
<div><span class="kicker">Cleaning</span><b>One row per day</b>
<ul><li>one price per zone and day</li><li>watch out for clock changes</li><li>put prices and weather side by side: 1,074 days</li></ul></div>
<div><span class="kicker">Analysis</span><b>Does wind matter?</b>
<ul><li>the gap: Malmö minus Luleå, each day</li><li>compare calm days with windy days</li><li>how sure can we be, and how much does weather explain?</li></ul></div>
<div class="result"><span class="kicker">Results</span><b>Partly</b>
<ul><li>Malmö 0.66, Luleå 0.31 kr/kWh on average</li><li>on calm days the gap is 0.40 kr/kWh bigger: not chance</li><li>but weather explains only about a fifth of it</li></ul></div>
:::

<p class="wfcode"><code>electricity/fetch_prices.py + fetch_weather.py</code> → <code>electricity/data/</code> → <code>electricity/report.qmd</code> → <code>report.md</code><span>one command: <code>uv run quarto render</code></span></p>

::: notes
Two sources, put side by side by date. The cleaning is where the work was; the next slides show it.
:::

## Four zones, one country

:::: cols
::: {}
- Since 2011 Sweden has **four price zones**, SE1 in the north to SE4 in the south.
- Much of the power is produced in the north, much of it used in the south.
- When the grid can't carry enough south, the prices split.
:::
::: {}
```{=html}
{{< include ../../public/img/introduction/diagram-zones.svg >}}
```
<p class="small muted">Mean spot price 2023–2025. Data: Nord Pool via elprisetjustnu.se.</p>
:::
::::

## The gap, month by month

<img src="../../img/introduction/electricity-zones.svg" alt="Monthly mean spot price in SE4 Malmö and SE1 Luleå, 2023–2025; Malmö is above Luleå almost every month">

<p class="small">The shaded area is the gap. Is it the wind? Wind power in the south should push southern prices down.</p>

::: notes
Sweden has four price zones since 2011. The gap is the shaded area. Question: how big is it,
and does it go with the weather? Wind power in the south should push southern prices down.
:::

## Where the work was: cleaning

```{=html}
{{< include ../../public/img/introduction/diagram-cleaning.svg >}}
```

::: twocol
- Prices came **every hour**, then from October 2025 **every 15 minutes**: a simple average counts them wrongly.
- Clocks change twice a year: some days have **23 or 25 hours**.
- Prices use world time, the weather Swedish dates: match them to the **right** day.
- **22 days** have no weather: dropped, and reported.
:::

<div class="keyline">None of this shows in the final figure. All of it changes the numbers if done wrong.</div>

::: notes
This is what combining sources really means. Each bullet is a bug that would silently shift
the result. The rendered report shows every one of these steps in code.
:::

## Calm days, big gap

<img src="../../img/introduction/electricity-wind.svg" alt="Mean price gap by wind quarter: 0.55 SEK per kWh on the calmest days, falling to 0.15 on the windiest">

On calm days the gap is **0.40 kr/kWh bigger** than on windy days, far more than chance would give. But wind and temperature explain only **18%** of the day-to-day gap.

::: notes
"Not chance" comes from a bootstrap interval (0.34–0.47), which you will see in the second half. The 18%: the rest is the
grid, nuclear maintenance and continental prices, which this data doesn't contain.
Correlation, not cause: windy days also differ in season and demand.
:::

## The maths: the gap, and how sure we are {.dense}

A day's price in zone $z$ is the average over its hours and quarter-hours, each counted by how long it lasted:

$$p_{z,d} = \frac{\sum_i \text{price}_i \cdot \text{minutes}_i}{\sum_i \text{minutes}_i} \qquad g_d = p_{\text{Malmö},d} - p_{\text{Luleå},d}$$

Compare the mean gap on the calmest and the windiest quarter of days:

$$\Delta = \bar g_{\text{calm}} - \bar g_{\text{windy}} = 0.55 - 0.15 = 0.40 \text{ kr/kWh}$$

- **How sure?** Redraw the days at random 10,000 times and recompute $\Delta$ each time: the middle 95% runs from 0.34 to 0.47. Zero is far outside, so it is not chance.
- **How much is weather?** Fit a straight line through wind and temperature:

$$g_d = a + b \cdot \text{wind}_d + c \cdot \text{temp}_d + \text{error}_d \qquad 1 - \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\text{error})}{\operatorname{Var}(g)} = 18\%$$

<p class="small">Each extra m/s of wind lowers the gap by 0.11 kr/kWh; wind and temperature together explain 18% of the day-to-day variation.</p>

::: notes
The resampling is the bootstrap (week 1, statistics). The fit is a linear regression; they will
meet it properly later. Here it is enough to say what each number means.
:::

# Is AI a bubble? {.divider}

<p class="muted">Ambitious project · three sources, and a question that needs work first</p>

## The workflow

::: workflow
<div><span class="kicker">Data</span><b>Three sources</b>
<ul><li>share prices vs company earnings, every month since 1871</li><li>the NASDAQ tech index since 1971</li><li>4.8 million headlines from Hacker News, a tech forum</li></ul></div>
<div><span class="kicker">Cleaning</span><b>Months, comparable</b>
<ul><li>line the three sources up month by month</li><li>read the dates carefully: one source writes October oddly</li><li>use shares of all headlines, not raw counts</li></ul></div>
<div><span class="kicker">Analysis</span><b>How unusual is today?</b>
<ul><li>turn "bubble" into three signs we can measure</li><li>how unusual is today, compared with every month before?</li><li>compare with 1929, 2000 and crypto</li></ul></div>
<div class="result"><span class="kicker">Results</span><b>Two of three signs</b>
<ul><li>valuations: higher than almost every month since 1871</li><li>attention: AI is in 14% of headlines; bitcoin peaked at 3%</li><li>price growth: ordinary (×1.6 in 5 years)</li></ul></div>
:::

<p class="wfcode"><code>ai-bubble/fetch.py</code> → <code>ai-bubble/data/</code> → <code>ai-bubble/report.qmd</code> → <code>report.md</code><span>one command: <code>uv run quarto render</code></span></p>

::: notes
The hard part here is the analysis step: deciding what to measure. The next slide shows how.
:::

## You can't measure a bubble, so measure its signs

```{=html}
{{< include ../../public/img/introduction/diagram-operationalise.svg >}}
```

- Nobody can observe "a bubble", and whether it bursts is a prediction, not a fact in a dataset.
- So we choose three **signs** people associate with bubbles, and ask how unusual today is on each, compared with 1929, 2000 and the crypto boom.

::: notes
This is the step that makes it ambitious: deciding what to measure. The data can't say
"bubble"; it can say how unusual today is on signs that people associate with bubbles.
:::

## Valuations: second only to 2000

<img src="../../img/introduction/ai-cape.svg" alt="Cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratio of US stocks since 1881, with 1929, 2000 and today marked; today is above 1929 and just below 2000">

<p class="small">US share prices compared with ten years of company earnings (Shiller's "CAPE"). Data: Robert Shiller.</p>

::: notes
Only the months around the 2000 peak were higher. 1929 was lower than today.
A cleaning trap: Shiller writes October as 2026.1, which as a number is the same as January.
:::

## Prices: an ordinary pace

<img src="../../img/introduction/ai-nasdaq.svg" alt="NASDAQ divided by its value five years earlier, since 1976; the 2000 peak is far higher than today">

<p class="small">The NASDAQ index divided by its value five years earlier. Data: FRED.</p>

<p>Today ×1.6: higher than only <b>40%</b> of months. In 2000: ×5.9. <span class="accent">This sign is not there.</span></p>

::: notes
This is the slide that makes the project honest. Showing only valuations and attention would make a
more exciting story and a less true one. Report the evidence that goes against you.
:::

## Attention: four times the crypto peak

<img src="../../img/introduction/ai-attention.svg" alt="Share of Hacker News story titles mentioning AI, bitcoin and crypto, 2007 to today; AI is far above the earlier crypto peaks">

<p class="small">Share of Hacker News headlines with each word. Data: Hacker News.</p>

## The honest answer

::: scorecard
<div class="yes"><span class="tick">✓</span><b>Valuations</b><span class="num">40.7</span><span class="muted">price vs earnings today · 44.2 in 2000</span></div>
<div class="yes"><span class="tick">✓</span><b>Attention</b><span class="num">14 %</span><span class="muted">of HN titles · bitcoin's peak: 3 %</span></div>
<div class="no"><span class="tick">✗</span><b>Price growth</b><span class="num">×1.6</span><span class="muted">in 5 years · ×5.9 in 2000</span></div>
:::

<p class="big" style="margin-top:.8em">Two of three signs are there. Whether a crash follows is <span class="accent">not in the data</span>.</p>

- High valuations can last for years; if AI raises earnings as expected, prices may be right.
- Three signs is our choice. US data, an English-language forum, few past bubbles to compare with.

::: notes
Ambition is not about a bigger dataset. It's about a question that takes real effort, results
that are checked, and conclusions that would convince a sceptical reader, including what you
can't conclude.
:::

## The maths: three signs, one question {.dense}

$$\text{valuation}_t = \frac{\text{price}_t}{\text{mean earnings, previous 10 years}} \qquad \text{growth}_t = \frac{\text{NASDAQ}_t}{\text{NASDAQ}_{t-5\text{ yrs}}}$$

$$\text{attention}_t = \frac{\text{headlines with “AI” in month } t}{\text{all headlines in month } t}$$

Each is compared with its own history. **How unusual is today?** The share of all earlier months with a lower value:

$$\text{rank} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{s=1}^{T} \mathbf{1}\{x_s < x_{\text{today}}\}$$

| Sign | Today | Rank | Record |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| valuation (CAPE) | 40.7 | 99% | 44.2, Dec 1999 |
| growth in 5 years | ×1.6 | 40% | ×5.9, Feb 2000 |
| attention | 13.7% | 97% | 15.9%, Feb 2026 |

::: notes
Prices and earnings are adjusted for inflation in Shiller's data. A rank of 99% means only 1% of
months since 1871 had a higher valuation.
:::

# How the course works {.divider}

## Six weeks, one cycle {.weeks}

Data science is the whole cycle: from a question, through messy real data, to an answer someone else can **check**.

| Week | Topic | Where it is in the cycle |
|:-|:-----------|:-------|
| 1 | Reproducible analysis: questions, Git and Quarto | the question · reproducible |
| 2 | Tables and plots | exploration |
| 3 | Cleaning and exploring messy data | cleaning · exploration |
| 4 | Combining data: joins and databases | data · cleaning |
| 5 | Data from the web | data |
| 6 | Text as data | data |

<p class="small">Statistics comes in every week: it is how you analyse and how sure you can be. You choose <b>Python or R</b>; everyone uses Quarto, Git and VS Code.</p>

<p class="more">More: <a href="../../about">About the course</a></p>

- **The proposal** names the group, the question and its data, and the grade you aim for. We check that the scope fits that grade.
- Same tools as the assignments: one repository per group, branches, pull requests, the check.
- Attending the presentations is compulsory.
